entry.title: The Boys at the Station: How Many Came Home? (No AI - WW1 Documentary)

media:group.media:title: The Boys at the Station: How Many Came Home? (No AI - WW1 Documentary)
media:group.media:description:
In August 1914, when Britain joined the First World War, men from across the country prepared to answer the call. But what actually became of them? In this video, we explore the fates of the men captured in a single photograph on a railway station platform in 1914, and ask the question: how many of them came home? Join us as we put names to faces, follow them to the trenches of the Western Front, and trace the lives of those who survived. This is the story of the Boys at the Station.

entry.title: Monte Cassino 1944: The Tank Assault Filmed by the Germans (No AI WW2 Documentary)

media:group.media:title: Monte Cassino 1944: The Tank Assault Filmed by the Germans (No AI WW2 Documentary)
media:group.media:description:
On 15th of February 1944, Allied bombers reduced the 1,500-year-old abbey of Monte Cassino to ruins, one of the most controversial decisions of the Second World War. This documentary examines the Battle of Monte Cassino from both sides, pairing Allied newsreels with rarely seen footage shot by German combat cameramen during the fighting.
Using wartime aerial photography laid over modern satellite imagery, the film shows why the Gustav Line made central Italy so formidable and why the road to Rome through the Liri Valley depended on taking the heights above Cassino. It follows the costly river crossings of January 1944, including the US 36th Texas Division’s assault on the Rapido and the French Colonial troops who came close to outflanking the entire position at Belvedere. It then turns to the bombing of the abbey, the street fighting in Cassino town against German paratroopers, the 4th Indian Division’s ordeal on Snakeshead Ridge, and the New Zealand tank assault up Cavendish Road toward Albaneta Farm, an action German newsreel cameras recorded as it unfolded. Along the way, the story connects Cassino to the stalemate at Anzio and builds toward Operation Diadem, the fourth battle, in which Polish, French, British, Canadian and American forces converged on the massif.
Fought over four months in mountains, rivers and rubble, Monte Cassino eventually drew in two entire Allied armies and soldiers from across the world. The destruction of the abbey is still debated today, and the battle remains central to how the Italian Campaign and its human cost are remembered.

entry.title: Only Three Survived: The True Story of the Goettge Patrol (No AI WW2 Documentary)

media:group.media:title: Only Three Survived: The True Story of the Goettge Patrol (No AI WW2 Documentary)
media:group.media:description:
Big thanks to VAER for sponsoring this video. Check them out and get a free watch roll with your purchase using this link: https://www.vaerwatches.com/battleguide
On the night of 12 August 1942, a 25-man US Marine patrol came ashore on Guadalcanal’s north coast hoping to find Japanese troops willing to surrender. By dawn, the Goettge Patrol had been almost entirely destroyed, and only three men made it back to American lines. This documentary reconstructs the disaster using survivor testimony, Japanese accounts, the 1st Marine Division’s D-2 journal, and the ground where it happened. It begins with Colonel Frank Goettge, the division’s intelligence officer, and a captured Japanese warrant officer whose interrogation suggested some enemy troops near the Matanikau River might give up. Goettge turned a planned combat patrol into a mission made up largely of mapmakers, photographers, a surgeon, a translator, and other specialists. They were lightly armed and carried no radio. Their boat then ran aground on a sandbar in the wrong place, east of Point Cruz, directly in front of a waiting Japanese force. We follow the fight on the beach and the escapes of Sergeant Charles “Monk” Arndt, Corporal Joseph Spaulding, and Platoon Sergeant Frank Few, each of whom swam and waded miles along the coast to reach safety. We also examine why the rescue force landed miles from the patrol, and what the official records left out.
The loss of the Goettge Patrol shaped the Guadalcanal campaign. It hardened Marine attitudes toward taking prisoners, stripped the division of intelligence specialists it couldn’t replace, and halted intelligence patrols for months. The men’s remains have never been found. The ground where they died now lies beneath Honiara, the capital of the Solomon Islands.

entry.title: The Destruction of Kampfgruppe Peiper (No AI Documentary)

media:group.media:title: The Destruction of Kampfgruppe Peiper (No AI Documentary)
media:group.media:description:
Our Book INFERNO is available now. Hardcover or eBook available on Amazon and Audiobook narrated by Dan: https://battleguide.co.uk/inferno
In December 1944, Kampfgruppe Peiper led Hitler's last great offensive in the West, spearheading the 1st SS Panzer Division's drive through the Ardennes. Using historical aerial imagery, veteran accounts and wartime combat footage, this documentary follows Joachim Peiper's armoured battle group across the Battle of the Bulge and asks how close it came to success.
Peiper's orders were to break through the American lines and seize the Meuse crossings at Huy and Amay within days. He commanded more than 800 vehicles, including Panthers, Panzer IVs and King Tiger heavy tanks, but they were confined to narrow roads, small bridges and a predetermined route through the Losheim Gap. His timetable began slipping from the first hours of the attack. A 22-man American reconnaissance platoon held Lanzerath for eight hours. The Germans captured a fuel depot at Büllingen. At the Baugnez crossroads, at least 84 American prisoners were murdered in what became known as the Malmedy Massacre. The film follows the fight for the bridge at Stavelot, the race to demolish the crossings at Trois Ponts and on the Lienne, and the battle for Stoumont, where the German spearhead met its strongest resistance yet.
The story of Kampfgruppe Peiper shows why the Ardennes offensive depended on speed, and why fuel shortages, terrain and an unrealistic timetable left so little margin for error. Above all, it reveals how small groups of American soldiers, engineers, gunners and rear-echelon troops, many of whom gave their lives, delayed the German advance long enough for reinforcements and Allied air power to decide the battle.

entry.title: Band of Brothers: The REAL Battle of Bloody Gulch (No AI Documentary)

media:group.media:title: Band of Brothers: The REAL Battle of Bloody Gulch (No AI Documentary)
media:group.media:description:
Huge thanks to VAER for sponsoring this video. Be sure to check them out, and get a free watch roll with your purchase by using this link: https://www.vaerwatches.com/battleguide
On 13th June 1944, German infantry and armour launched a ferocious counterattack against American paratroopers on the outskirts of Carentan, Normandy. This video reconstructs the Battle of Bloody Gulch using eyewitness accounts, wartime records and original 1944 aerial photography to reveal what really happened, field by field.
Band of Brothers made Easy Company's stand at Carentan famous, but the true story is far more complex. When the German attack came, Easy Company wasn't even in the front line. It was Dog and Fox Companies of the 506th Parachute Infantry Regiment who bore the initial assault, fighting and dying for hours before the line came close to collapse entirely.
Using Lt Ronald Speirs' original battle map overlaid onto historic reconnaissance photography, this video pinpoints the actual location of the fighting, correcting decades of misidentification, including on Google Earth, and traces the chaotic withdrawal of F Company, the isolation of Speirs' platoon at an exposed farmhouse, and the desperate defence that held the American line until 2nd Armored Division tanks arrived to turn the tide.
Beyond the famous television dramatisation lies a battle involving far more men than a single company: paratroopers from the 501st and 502nd, tank crews, mortar teams and medics, all fighting to prevent a German breakthrough that could have unravelled the entire Normandy campaign. Understanding what actually happened at Bloody Gulch restores a fuller, more accurate picture of one of the 101st Airborne Division's hardest-fought engagements, and honours the men whose contribution has often been overshadowed by a more famous few.

entry.title: The Death of Joachim Peiper: The Crime Scene Evidence (No AI Documentary)

media:group.media:title: The Death of Joachim Peiper: The Crime Scene Evidence (No AI Documentary)
media:group.media:description:
On the night of 13-14 July 1976, in rural France, former Waffen-SS colonel Joachim Peiper was killed when unknown attackers set fire to his home. Peiper, convicted of war crimes for the Malmedy massacre and sentenced to death, had spent twenty years living quietly in the village of Traves, until his identity was exposed. Using surviving police files, crime-scene photographs, and archival material rarely examined together, this video reconstructs the final hours of his life in unprecedented detail.
We trace how Peiper built a secluded home in the French countryside, how a local newspaper exposed his wartime past, and how death threats and a hostile press campaign closed in during the summer of 1976. Drawing on original police plans, ballistics reports, and eyewitness depositions, we map the attackers' route to his property, the gunfire exchanged that night, and the fire that ultimately killed him. We also examine the identification of his remains, which put decades of escape rumors to rest, and the police investigation that followed, from a suspicious neighbor to a group of local youths, none of whom were ever charged.
The murder of Joachim Peiper remains officially unsolved. His case sits at the uneasy intersection of justice, vigilantism, and unresolved history, raising difficult questions about accountability decades after the Second World War ended. Nearly fifty years on, newly surfaced evidence allows this story to be told with more precision than ever before, offering a rare, detailed look at how the war's legacy continued to shape lives, and claim them, long after 1945.

entry.title: Iwo Jima Cave Ambush: New Evidence After 80 Years (No AI)

media:group.media:title: Iwo Jima Cave Ambush: New Evidence After 80 Years (No AI)
media:group.media:description:
On March 3, 1945, Marine combat cameraman Sergeant William "Bill" Genaust walked into a cave on Iwo Jima and was never seen again. This investigation reconstructs, for the first time, the final moments of the man whose eight seconds of film immortalized the raising of the flag on Mount Suribachi.
Genaust landed on Iwo Jima's Green Beach on day one, filming the chaos of the invasion before capturing the second flag raising alongside photographer Joe Rosenthal. Weeks later, while filming an experimental flamethrowing tank, he joined a small intelligence patrol investigating a cave on Hill 362A. What happened next has been obscured for eighty years by conflicting death certificates, mislabeled unit muster rolls, and a caption error that sent researchers to the wrong hill entirely. By cross-referencing an unpublished memoir from the officer who survived the ambush with six overlooked photographs taken by fellow cameraman Bob Campbell, this investigation identifies the true location of Genaust's final patrol, traces the geological features still visible on the hillside today, and examines the 2007 military search that came within a meter of the answer.
Genaust's disappearance is more than a footnote to a famous photograph. He was among the most decorated combat cameramen of the Pacific War, and his remains are one of thousands still missing from Iwo Jima. This investigation is being submitted to the Defense POW/MIA Accounting Agency in the hope that renewed analysis, using modern LiDAR and photogrammetry, can finally bring him home.

entry.title: The Explosion of HMS Barham: Frame by Frame (No AI Documentary)

media:group.media:title: The Explosion of HMS Barham: Frame by Frame (No AI Documentary)
media:group.media:description:
This extraordinary footage is among the most famous, and tragic, pieces of naval film of the Second World War: A British battleship, heavily listing to port, her crew racing along the capsizing hull, before a massive explosion sends her to the bottom of the Mediterranean. Yet, while these scenes are widely known, they leave behind a number of powerful questions: how did HMS Barham meet her end? What caused that catastrophic explosion? Why did she sink so quickly? And what became of those men aboard one of Britain’s most famous battleships?
Join us in this video as, using eyewitness accounts previously unseen Kriegsmarine records, and the footage itself, we forensically reconstruct one of the Royal Navy's greatest wartime disasters.

entry.title: Following a Fallen Cameraman Into the Hell of Saipan (No AI Documentary)

media:group.media:title: Following a Fallen Cameraman Into the Hell of Saipan (No AI Documentary)
media:group.media:description:
Huge thanks to VAER for sponsoring this video. Check out their outstanding collection of watches right here: https://vaer-watches.sjv.io/battleguide
Saipan, 9th July 1944. Shortly after 2pm, a Marine Corps cameraman filmed the American flag being raised over the newly captured Marpi Airfield. To the exhausted Marines watching below, it seemed the battle for Saipan was finally over. Just a few hours later, the man who captured this film was dead. But how did a young Marine cameraman, recommended for the Navy Cross, survive one of the Pacific War's bloodiest battles, only to lose his life at the point of victory?

entry.title: The Battle of the Somme: The Final Attack (No AI)

media:group.media:title: The Battle of the Somme: The Final Attack (No AI)
media:group.media:description:
Shout-out to the A Family History of… podcast for supporting this video. In their latest episode, they tell the moving story of the Attenborough brothers. Three went to war, and two were killed on the Somme just twelve days apart.
Watch here: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=UhV2Y6uyabg&list=PL1lWcWnOjhe_Bs1UpzOYeWNgIlmoOHGrB&index=2
Ask somebody in the street today about the Battle of the Somme and one date inevitably comes up: 1st July 1916. And for good reason. It was the bloodiest day in the history of the British Army, with nearly 60,000 casualties and more than 19,000 dead. But the Somme was not a one-day battle. The fighting continued for another four months and by November the battlefield had become a hellish wasteland of mud, shell holes and unburied dead. Yet still the attacks went on. With all sides on the verge of total exhaustion, the British would launch one final major assault in the hope of making one final advance before winter closed in.
In this video, with the help of rare battlefield footage filmed at the time, we're going to explore that much-overlooked final phase of the Somme, in which exhausted men fought in horrific conditions to rescue victory from the jaws of defeat.

media:group.media:title: The Day German Bombers Appeared Over London (No AI Documentary)
media:group.media:description:
On 13 June 1917, London experienced its first major daylight bombing raid when German Gotha bombers crossed the North Sea and attacked the capital. In less than twenty minutes, 162 people were killed and hundreds more injured, including children at the Upper North Street School in Poplar. This episode explores how the raid unfolded, why London's defences failed, and how the attack marked a turning point in the history of modern warfare.

media:group.media:title: The Battle of Beersheeba (WW1 Documentary) No AI
media:group.media:description:
PLAUD Note Pro helps record, transcribe, summarise, and organise field notes, interviews, and research. BATTLE15 FOR 15% OFF Amazon: https://amzn.to/4ewlGPp Website: https://bit.ly/PlaudBattleGuideVT
On October 31, 1917, hundreds of Australian horsemen charged straight into Ottoman trenches at the Battle of Beersheba, one of the last great cavalry charges in modern warfare. By this stage of the First World War, cavalry was supposed to be obsolete. So how did this attack succeed, and why did it matter so much to the campaign for Jerusalem?
This video uses aerial reconnaissance photos, wartime maps, and firsthand letters and diaries to reconstruct the battle in detail. It follows the ANZAC advance through the Sinai desert, the stalled British campaign that made Beersheba a target, and the German-led Ottoman defenses built around the town's water wells, railway, and the commanding height of Tel el Saba. Personal accounts bring the human side of the battle into focus, including cricketer-turned-soldier Tibby Cotter and Trooper Randolph Cleaver, who was denied leave to see his dying father just days before the attack. As the sun set on October 31st, Australian General Harry Chauvel made a decision that sent the 4th Light Horse Brigade galloping across six kilometers of open desert toward a line of Ottoman rifles and artillery.
The Battle of Beersheba broke a months-long stalemate in the Sinai and Palestine Campaign and opened the road to Jerusalem, making it a turning point in Britain's war against the Ottoman Empire. It also stands as one of history's final large-scale mounted charges, a moment when nineteenth-century tactics briefly triumphed against modern firepower before that kind of warfare disappeared for good.

Twice in the space of just 30 years, humanity fought wars on a scale never seen before. Millions died, empires collapsed, and nations were transformed. But out of the hundreds of battles fought across those conflicts, which ones truly shaped the world we live in today? That question lies at the heart of Inferno, a brand-new book examining the battles we believe defined the 20th century.
Written by four historians, each bringing their own unique perspective, Inferno explores war on land, at sea, and in the air — from Mons in 1914 and the trenches of the Somme, to Stalingrad, Normandy, and the brutal final battles of the Pacific War. entry.title: Meuse-Argonne: Investigating America's Bloodiest 47 Days (No AI Documentary)

media:group.media:title: Meuse-Argonne: Investigating America's Bloodiest 47 Days (No AI Documentary)
media:group.media:description:
The Meuse-Argonne was the largest battle in American history, involving over a million US soldiers, yet few people today have even heard of it. This video explores why this brutal 47-day campaign, fought across the Argonne Forest and the banks of the Meuse River in the final months of World War One, deserves to be remembered alongside Gettysburg and D-Day.
In September 1918, General John Pershing sent an inexperienced American Expeditionary Force against some of the most heavily fortified German positions on the Western Front. Colonel George Marshall faced the near-impossible task of repositioning 600,000 men in under two weeks. The advance stalled at the fortress hill of Montfaucon, where German machine guns tore through the attacking divisions. In the Argonne Forest, Major Charles Whittlesey's men became trapped behind enemy lines in what became known as the Lost Battalion, while Corporal Alvin York, a reluctant soldier from rural Tennessee, carried out the actions that would earn him the Medal of Honor. A young George Patton was cut down leading tanks into battle, and future OSS founder William Donovan showed remarkable courage under fire.
By the time the fighting ended alongside the armistice on 11th November 1918, the Meuse-Argonne had cost 26,000 American lives, making it deadlier day-for-day than Normandy in the Second World War. More than a costly victory, it marked the moment the American Army transformed from an untested force into one capable of modern industrial warfare, a transformation that shaped how the United States would fight in the decades that followed.
